title: A more diverse eligible electorate does not automatically mean more political power
source_unit: Pew Research Center analysis of American Community Survey/IPUMS data and Census-based population projections
geography: United States citizens age 18 and older in the 50 states and District of Columbia

denominator.unit: U.S. eligible voters; group shares use Pew's displayed four-group reporting universe

observations.method: Pew analysis of ACS/IPUMS data for 2006-2024 with 2026 projections based on Census Vintage 2025 population estimates and Census population projections.
observations.uncertainty: 2026 national figures are projections; displayed four-group shares omit other or multiple-race categories, and the analysis does not incorporate citizens abroad or all state-specific disenfranchisement rules.
observations.subgroup: White, Hispanic, Black, and Asian eligible voters as defined by Pew; Hispanics may be of any race, while White, Black, and Asian groups are non-Hispanic single-race categories.
observations.counterinterpretation: A changing eligible-voter composition changes the formal electorate but does not by itself change registration, turnout, representation, party alignment, policy influence, or legitimacy.

observations.method: Pew comparison of 2022 ACS-based counts with 2026 Census-based projections; counts are rounded and percentages use unrounded values.
observations.uncertainty: The source attributes growth to adulthood and naturalization patterns but does not follow individuals into registration, voting, or political representation.
observations.subgroup: Eligible-voter groups defined by Pew's racial and ethnic reporting categories.
observations.counterinterpretation: Population growth or naturalization can expand formal electoral presence without equal political voice if registration, access, turnout, representation, or issue alignment differs.

observations.period: 2024; share of adults eligible to vote by group

denominator.unit: adults in each Pew racial and ethnic reporting group

white_eligible_share.unit: percent of White adults eligible to vote

black_eligible_share.unit: percent of Black adults eligible to vote

hispanic_eligible_share.unit: percent of Hispanic adults eligible to vote

asian_eligible_share.unit: percent of Asian adults eligible to vote

observations.method: Pew analysis of 2024 ACS data using age and citizenship to define eligibility.
observations.uncertainty: Eligibility shares reflect age and citizenship composition and do not identify barriers, preferences, registration, or turnout.
observations.subgroup: Pew racial and ethnic reporting groups among U.S. adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different eligibility shares do not by themselves show unequal political commitment or exclusion; they describe who is a citizen adult and therefore in the formal electorate.

related_sources.claim: The analysis uses American Community Survey data as a major historical source.

boundary: This record measures the changing racial and ethnic composition of the formal eligible electorate and group-specific eligibility shares. It does not measure registration, ballot access, turnout, representation, party preference, policy influence, political efficacy, or legitimacy; 2026 national values are projections and four-group displays omit other or multiple-race categories.
